text_fidelity_a:
Kodak PlaySport (Zx3) HD Waterproof Pocket Video Camera (Purple) There's a lot to like about the Playsport. For one, it's very easy to use as a point and shoot should be. The picture quality is certainly fine for just about anybody's use, save for those who really like blowing their pictures up large. It's very fast to move between photos and movie--a few thumb moves is all it takes. The same for toggling between the movie quality. Which means if you suddenly want to grab a still photo while videoing or are worried about recording room and want to drop down a notch or two in quality, you can do so without missing a lot of action. The zoom is a 3X, which is serviceable. I'd prefer longer and I'm sure the next version will offer a longer zoom, but as I use this for quick shots of the family and not for event shooting, the 3X is rarely an issue in terms of not being adequate.

Transfer of files is easy and fast (I use a Mac) and all the cables come bundled with it. Yes, you read that right--it ships with all the needed cables.

Because it is so small and slim, and held in that vertical position, it can get a bit shaky and you'll need to pay attention to keeping it steady, more so than larger cameras or ones you hold with two hands horizontally. The sound pickup is fine save that wind noise can be a problem on windy days--it'll wash out a good deal of the speaking sound.

It feels rugged out of the box and the number of times I've dropped it, including just recently while chasing my boy and his friend around the corner of the house and getting my foot caught in the extension cord of the Halloween decorations. I watched the camera skid across several feet of concrete sidewalk but it was none the worse for wear.

It's slimness makes it a great pocket camera--one of those where it's defined as such not because you can cram it into your pocket and walk around like you have a grapefruit in there but where it slips right in and you barely notice it. That's one of the reasons it's become the camera I take most often when I know I won't need a larger zoom or a flash.

I haven't tried the underwater aspect in actual underwater conditions (snorkeling, say), but a few practice photos in the pool shows it takes pretty sharp photos in that environment. But I'll leave the gauging of that aspect to those more well-versed in such a need.

In the end, it's a great little camera and as mentioned, it's quickly become the one I carry along most often when we're just heading out for some family fun. For post-dusk indoor, I take a Canon elph and for events or hiking a Canon IS with a 12x zoom and a tele-converter. But for playing games in the yard, birthday parties, classroom events, etc.--the Kodak has become the go-to camera.

highly recommended
text_fidelity_b: Kodak PlaySport (Zx3) HD Waterproof Pocket Video Camera (Purple)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch Immediately, I realized I love these headphones. I'm not in love with the color, and I'm perplexed why companies always say something is for iPad, etc., although I suspect it is just the "cool" thing to do. I have no apple devices, but this worked immediately and perfectly for my Blackberry 9700, Xoom, and Win7 Laptop.

The first device pairs by itself, and devices 2-8 pair by holding 2 buttons for 5 seconds. After that, if multiple devices are turned on when you turn the headphones on, it seems to want to pick the first one you paired it with.

The BB picks it up as a Logitech Wireless Headset (not something generic), and you can then control the volume with the BB or with the headset itself (Did I mention the controls are all well positioned on the right headphone? - just two volume buttons, mic mute, micro USB charging port, and LED indicator), and you can also toggle between BB speaker phone and headset - they are obviously fully compatible - not generically. Pressing the mute button give you an audible cue, but does not change the BB display.

You'll never catch me in public with a normal bluetooth earpiece on anyway, so this is also great for calls at home - it will cancel out more background noise (because of the foam on both ears) so you can comfortably concentrate on your call. My tests show it working well more than the claimed 10m away (of course that partly depends on the other device's radio as well).

As another reviewer said, these sound good (and are capable of getting louder than I'll ever need), but are probably not as great as the full over-the-ear headsets. BUT, the wireless capability is really great to keep you fully uninhibited when exercising, cooking, or whatever you're doing when talking on the phone or listening to your music. For the record, I am 100% opposed to wireless shelf/tower speakers in a real home system, but this is a great solution for a headset.

Also, the mic backing out of the way is a must, so thankfully that is included. It not only pivots, but flexes toward or away from the mouth as well - very good design. Finally, the folding feature is great; any space saved is important. And the connecting wire connecting the two sides is accessible, if all that bending ever has it in need of a replacement.

Past helmet use has me thinking my skull is about as large as they come, and these are comfortable on me with the sides fully extended.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Wireless Headset for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch

Dell i5675-A933BLU-PUS Inspiron 5675 AMD Desktop, Ryzen 5 1400 Processor, 8GB, 1TB, AMD Radeon RX 570 4GB GDDR5 Graphics, Recon Blue As someone who generally builds their own computer, this was somewhat of an experiment for me. It's always been my opinion that pre-built machines focus on the specs of a few key components and then skimp on the rest. I can't say this machine changed my mind on that, but it is nice for most people, who don't want to figure out how to make their own to have something already together that just works.

So far, I've used it for a few months and haven't had any failures. It's handled software installations, Windows updates, and new hardware with a minimum of errors. The card readers work. The ports are easy to reach. it isn't especially noisy, but it's far from silent. I've used it for mild gaming, some CAD design work with a program that often crashes and is a ram-hog, and general browing and have had no lagging or problems. Seems to work great!

In my haste to get rid of pre-installed software, I removed the software that turns the light in the DELL logo on and off on the front. I had turned it off, but as soon as I rebooted, it came on and stayed that way. The wires don't seem to be easily accessible to unplug it. I don't consider a bright blue glowing logo that defaults to on to be an added value to the customer, but I guess I'm not really surprised.

Positives:
- It is what it looks like, does what it claims to do, and basically works
- cheap
- comes with an AC adapter!! Wow. You can pay a lot for a light that doesn't

Negatives: I'm using this for Macro work (I'm new to macro) so that's the perspective I'm coming from
- Not Bright Enough! It's just not all that bright. Not enough to light a subject by itself for macro purposes. I doubt it's adequate for more than a highlight for portraiture. This is why 2 stars. If a light doesn't light - it's not a light.

Really that's it. This is not a knock to the light (and not why I gave it a low rating), but if you are planning on using it for macro, buy a flash instead. A flash will not only have higher output, but will help freeze the camera shake (a big macro problem). Also, I thought the full time light would be better for live insects (you can see what you're doing!), but it's the opposite. You need the flash to freeze action. Not a criticism (this light does not advertise itself as a flash), but something to know.

UPDATE: I used it a couple more times. I am finding it more useful than initially when very close in. I would still strongly recommend a flash for this unless you have a compelling reason for continuous illumination (e.g you're waiting for a bug to crawl into frame and it's too dark to see otherwise. Though the lights would probably scare the bug). If you have a pretty solid tripod setup, this can work for longer exposure macro. Not great though. Upped to 3 stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging I have a Nuvi 360. It came with a suction cup windshield mount. It also came with a steel disk with double sticky adhesive on the back. I was supposed to mount this disk somewhere on my dashboard, then use the suction cup to attach the mount. I didn't want to use the suction mount directly onto the windshield because 1) it telegraphs the presence of an expensive GPS unit, 2) it's illegal in California to attach anything to the windshield and 3) I don't think the suction cup would last very long.

Then there's the disk with the very permanent double sticky tape. The problem with almost all cars these days is there really isn't anywhere to attach the disk discreetly. Every square inch is taken with existing stuff. And who wants an ugly disk glued to the dash anyway? And what if I want to use the GPS in other vehicles? More disks?

So I settled on this "beanbag" mount with the ball mount arm.

Unfortunately, before the beanbag friction mount arrived, I was flexing the arm in the suction cup mount and noticed the suction cup's mounting bracket had already broken. I had never even attached it to anything! The mount is beautifully engineered and built...except for one area where the arm's hinge pin attaches to the suction cup's plastic hinge loops. The loops are too thin and fragile. The loops cracked and broke with hardly any hinging at all.

So now I have a quite useless suction mount but a very functional ball arm. What to do?

I drove the hinge pin out of the ball arm. Then I took two small 1" x 1" steel angle brackets and attached them to the ball arm with a 2" long, 8-32 threaded machine screw and an 8-32 wingnut. This created two "feet" for the ball arm. Then I epoxied the two bracket "feet" to the fabric (upper) side of an old 1/4" thick mousepad. Ta da. A friction pad for pennies with a ball arm attached.

Works great. Cost was virtually nothing. Doesn't slide on either of the two dashboards I've tried it on. The mousepad is flexible and conforms easily to the curving shape of the various dashboards. It doesn't weigh much but the thick mousepad has enough heft to plant the getup nicely. The grippy rubber side of the mousepad adheres nicely to the dash. Yet I can pull it down to the floor quickly and reposition it easily.

I wish I'd thought of this BEFORE I ordered this "official" friction mount to the tune of a couple of twenties.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging

iHome Smart Brief: 13 inch Laptop Briefcase for Mac, Heathered Grey Last year I switched to a Macbook Pro 13-inch after being a PC user since the early eighties. I love my Mac, but I haven't gone whole-hog for the rest of the pricey iProducts Apple puts out. Still, this case is just about perfect for my needs.

First, I like how the zippered compartment for the computer does not unzip all around. It's really easy to slip my Mac in and out of its fleecy padded pocket while still feeling like it's protected. (There's also plenty of room for my little wireless mouse dongle, although I don't use a mouse much anymore.) The iPad compartment is similar, and it holds my Kindle Fire in its rooCase with room to spare for something else (like a checkbook or wallet perhaps). The clever half-case compartment with pockets for chargers, headphones, and pens has plenty of room for my Mac power supply, Kindle charger and cables, and another charger if I need it.

The full compartment in the middle of the case is for whatever you might stick in it. It's not huge in depth, but it would certainly hold a legal pad/portfolio and a magazine or two. I don't use a cell phone now, but one day I might, so the outer pocket for the phone is nice; it's also serviceable for one of those small flashlights or perhaps a set of keys (on the right keychain). Toothbrush! I could see using the sleeve as a lapdesk/laptop stand while seated on a plane or in a doctor's office.

The sleeve comes with a classy, comfortable shoulder strap with strong, reliable clips. At first it wasn't clear what the the clips were supposed to clip to, but they are hidden away under the edges of the center gusset (what you see as the narrow black line running across the thickness in the photo here). There's no tangling up with this shoulder strap, either; the business ends can be rotated to keep the strap straight.

It's lightweight. And the color? It's a perfect match for the Mac Lion startup screen, of course. Everything about it says "Mac," including the iHome logo, but you don't have to be an Apple nut to love this sleeve. Very well designed.
text_fidelity_b: iHome Smart Brief: 13 inch Laptop Briefcase for Mac, Heathered Grey

Panasonic HomeHawk Outdoor Wireless Smart Home Security Camera, Wide Angle View, Color Night Vision, 2-Way Talk, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, 1 Camera Kit (KX-HN7001W) The Panasonic HomeHawk system has its good and its areas that could use some upgrades.
The good:
This is about as simple and install as you will get for a home monitoring system. No wires, five screws, charging the camera, downloading the app and you are ready to go, it is that simple. Once the cameras are charged and mounted I think it took me about 5 minutes to get everything running, and I am not technical by any stretch of the imagination.
The cameras are clear and provide good picture (you can select the quality of the picture when setting the system up) of the areas they are monitoring. Recordings are of good quality and clear, the night recording can be either color or black and white (infrared) depending on your choice.
Recording trigger areas can be set up along with sensitivity to movement in the recording area to trigger the recording to begin. All of these are very handy and easy to use.
The app is simple to use and pretty intuitive on how the system operates allowing almost everyone to use the system without any special knowledge. In all a good system for 95% of the people out there.
The things that can be improved.
It became apparent during setup of the outdoor camera (the one that looks like ET) that you need to mount it in a specific orientation, if you turn it over you cannot flip the image and everything will be upside down. If the ball neck for mounting the camera was just a little longer this would not be an issue as you could fit it under a soffit on your house wit a large field of view.
On the outdoor camera it works best when the rear of the camera is pointed in the direction of the base unit for connectivity. As you turn the camera and point the rear away from the base the signal drops pretty quick and the camera will not connect.
Other than these items the system is pretty easy to set up and use, now we see all the raccoons that show up to the house at night.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic HomeHawk Outdoor Wireless Smart Home Security Camera, Wide Angle View, Color Night Vision, 2-Way Talk, Works with Alexa & Google Assistant, 1 Camera Kit (KX-HN7001W)

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation Great wireless camera/doorbell. Hardware/software this is ideal. We live on a busy street so we were getting lots of notifications. The software allowed us to adjust where the camera sensed motion, cutting down "false" notifications. Easy to use.
Easy to setup and install. Took maybe 15 minutes from opening the box to having it up and running.
Convenient set-up and access via phone (iOS and Android) app. Added skill to Echo, so when someone sets of camera or pushes doorbell, we get a notification via Alexa, and an image on the Echo show. You can adjust how often and what notifications you receive in the app.
Night vision is pretty good as well. Another nice feature is you can access a "live" view anytime, notification or not.
Audio works well, so if you are in the basement, garage, at work, shopping you can talk to whomever is at your door.
If you carry your phone everywhere or have a smart home speaker (Google, Echo or maybe Apple?) you won't need the additional chime, phone and speakers have a decently loud sound.
I would suggest getting a second battery if you have a busy street or lots of activity. The app notifies you in plenty of time the battery is low and needs to be recharged (only takes a couple hours to fully charge). But a second battery extends the life and less work (but to be fair, one screw using included driver, slide off plate, slide battery out, set to charge and reverse process to put battery back in. With two batteries, the whole thing takes about two minutes. With one, you simply have a non-functioning doorbell/camera for a few hours. No biggie, just FYI.
Also there is an an App called Neighbors free to join and use. It lets you share "videos and notifications of criminal or suspicious activity. So if someone in your neighborhood is broken into or home is vandalized they can share the video and/or share a notice of the incident. Lost dog, share. Delivery thieves, share. So both kinda cool and scary.
Now the BAD. To access the video you have to pay a monthly fee ( now if you access the video within the first 30 seconds or so, you are golden, but if you have your hands full, or can't access your phone, you can't see the video, or back it up. While the basic few is like $40 ish a year. Higher for the next tier up. That is forever. And no easy way to back up to a local storage device. All files are on Rings servers.
Now if you know that up front, and $40 is no biggie. Then 5 stars.
But for me that is an issue.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation

The technology is great when it's working, but, for whatever reason, my system has needed to be reset once a week or more, and the coverage is nowhere near as good as it claims it should be.

My hope was that the newer version would be faster and have better coverage. It isn't. It doesn't. And, like the earlier version, it has to be in AP mode to work with my FIOS modem (FIOS has a version of this available with its own firmware, but you have to buy a new one, and it won't work with any other ISP). Those hopes dashed, my next hope was that I could at least use the router as a satellite on my existing system, which, of course not.

So, you would think I could at LEAST use the satellite from the new one with the old system or the old satellite with the new one? They are the same model, after all. And that, too, would be a nope.

What I finally did, after hours on the internet (and other hours just trying to set up the new one by itself - it was the same with the old one - it for some reason despises custom settings and will not save them the first many times. It will also lose them after firmware upgrades, I expect, like its predecessor), was set it up alongside the old one with its own network name. Now I have one network serving one side of the house and the other serving the other. Speeds are good. So far, no routing issues, and I don't really expect any. The two network solution seems to have worked well for others.

But really.

If you are looking to expand your Orbi network, check out the nighthawk mesh expanders. I have the 7500, and it's excellent. Also, don't take my lukewarm review for a no-rec. The Orbi is, as far as I can tell from personal experience, buggy and locked down, but, again from personal experience, it beats the Velop (its nearest competitor) by a mile for coverage.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Orbi Compact Wall-Plug Whole Home Mesh WiFi System - WiFi router and wall-plug satellite extender with speeds up to 2.2 Gbps over 3,500 sq. feet, AC2200 (RBK20W)

text_fidelity_a:
WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD UPDATE: Since the review below this paragraph, I have put this up without a backup, and it's been a fire and forget mission. No problems with wireless network service. My "OK" review still stands, but I'm still optimistic some firmware upgrades or a big "that's it!" on my end could get everything working better or even flawlessly.

I have an extensive wired gigabit network in my home, so it has not been my top priority to replace my antiquated wireless B/G router (although I do use it much for casual surfing, mind you). Because I've been very busy when at home lately and in no mood to deal with nuisance computer/network issues, I put this new router in parallel with the old so that if issues came up, I wouldn't have to deal with them immediately. After about three weeks, albeit with only casual and sporadic "trying to make it work right", it's still not ready to run solo, obviously reason enough to just rate average.

This is unfortunate because it has a lot of cool touted features. The funny thing is when I was first setting it up I was thinking how they really have it idiot-proofed - even the WAN port is color coded to the included network cable (they don't even call it a WAN port, BTW).

But as is so often the case, by trying to make something useable to the masses, it actually becomes more difficult for advanced users to do simple tasks: I sort of want some Network Attached Storage (NAS), but have been too cheap/lazy/power misery to want to bother dealing with it, so I thought it would be great to try this router with its USB ports - ideally, I was going to put some hard drives in my gun safe, which is beside my telecom closet, and attach them to the router via USB, and have them both set to turn off when not in use. But it's just not working. I could go into a rant here about how Windows tries to set up a GUI so that people ignorant to computers can access their media when I all I really want to do is access the root of the drives and then do what I want without interference, but I'll save you my usual rant because I don't want you to misinterpret that it is indeed the router's fault that it rarely recognizes my attached devices (although interaction with various versions of Windows is the fault of both companies). The fact is, from the router's access page, you can see that my drives are often not recognized at all, or the router still thinks I have something attached that I've detached a while back (and sometimes even after a reboot). Clearly, I'm not about to put these drives down in a safe on another floor; it's easier just to deal with them locally. I was unable to EVER access these from a tablet or a phone; I wasn't about to waste that much time when I couldn't even rely on it to work with decent Windows machines.

The gigabit Ethernet ports are a great feature, and the wireless portion works better, but there have been a few times where I've checked my machines and they've reverted back to my legacy network, meaning that the new router obviously went down, if only for a short time. Thus, I'm not ready to put this machine up solo and deal with any headaches that I may have to incur.

With some cool features like QoS (Quality of Service) and port forwarding, etc., it sounds like it could be a great router. I can't begin to test these well when I'm still frustrated with making it look like a real seamless network. These are probably things that can and will be fixed with firmware updates, but they should have had this ironed out before release. If I hear of a good update, I'll give it another go if I'm still interested and will let you know how it works out.
text_fidelity_b: WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD

text_fidelity_a:
Pentax K100D Super 6.1MP Digital SLR Camera Shake Reduction and 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Lens First of all, I would like to start with highly recommending this camera to ANYONE who wants premium image quality with expandability, power and flexibility.

Pentax is one of the only companies out there that is driven entirely by photography and NOT by a marketing department that makes outrageous claims. To this end, even this, their lowest-end camera, is PACKED with premium features. Let's take a look at them:

1. Dust Reduction: Dust WILL get into your camera! This keeps it off of the sensor and increases the time inbetween cleanings.

2. Shake Reduction: It's good for a couple of stops of shooting leeway and you get it with every lens you use. Other companies build their systems into the lenses, meaning ONE lens can cost as much or more than the camera, itself! Lens-based anti-shake systems are more effective at long zoom than body-based systems, but unless you're rich, you won't be able to afford a suite of good lenses! With this camera, you can use ANY Pentax lens and get anti-shake.

3. AA batteries: Proprietary battery packs are NO GOOD. Hmmm, if you're on a shoot and your pack dies, you're not taking ANY photos unless you get a spare, right? With this camera, pick up some 2500mAh Ni-MH AA's and you can afford to get three sets. However, the power drain is so small, you might not need more than one set.

4. 6 MP sensor: Don't EVER get trapped in the megapixel hype. Megapixels mean nothing in the DSLR game, except for noise issues. Let me explain. The sensor sizes on almost all DSLRs (except for $5000 full-frame pro cameras) are APS-sized, meaning the sensor size on this camera and the Nikon D300 are very nearly the same dimensions. This means that photosensors on the chip have to be made smaller to get more pixels...meaning that the closer together/smaller sites are LESS light sensitive and they will also interfere with each other. 6 MP is a perfect sweet spot for noise and image sharpness. You get a base ISO of 200, meaning your camera is TWICE as sensitive to light as one with a base ISO of 100! This camera records color accurately and makes prints up to 8.5"x11" with no problem.

This camera has huge features and, even with the release of the K20D and K200D cameras, still maintains a good feature/image quality set with a proven CCD sensor and a suite of easy-to-learn features and settings. I LOVE this camera and even though I have a K200D for the weather sealing and larger burst capacity, the K100D super is the camera I ALWAYS take with me in trips. You're better off getting this camera plus a really nice lens and a 360FZ flash than a more expensive camera with a base kit lens and no external flash.

Believe me, this camera's quality will not fail to impress you and it will grow with you. It can use ANY lens its bigger brothers can and it uses them effortlessly.

A superb camera and one for the record books!
text_fidelity_b: Pentax K100D Super 6.1MP Digital SLR Camera Shake Reduction and 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Lens

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0 Comcast has repeatedly lied to me, sending me letters and alerts telling me that I need a new cable modem or my service will be seriously degraded. One time they went so far as to set a date when my service would NO longer work at all! Of course, I would never believe them without double-checking for myself, and I found out it was indeed an outright lie. Even the oldest DOCSIS versions can handle more than my 30Mbps connection. I suppose the lie was because they want me to rent their modem for $10 or more a month and relinquish control of my own network to them.

That said, it makes sense to upgrade when convenient to be sure you're future proofed. Eventually even the cheapest Internet plans will be upgraded to higher speeds. When I heard that I could register this on Comcast's network online without having to call them (and have them speak extremely condescendingly to me even though I'm a Systems Engineer), I was sold. Worth doing.

Note that just because DOCSIS 3.0 can reach speeds of 10Gbps with maxed out number of channels, this modem is 680Mbps, which will be out of date eventually, when we finally get Gigabit Ethernet to residences.

Another (of a million) thing(s) I hate about Comcast is that they by default use your AP (that they rent to you as part of a router/AP/modem combo) to create a public (virtual) wireless AP for their other customers. They say this will not affect your bandwidth, but it can affect your throughput. And it uses your electricity. And why would you want to help Comcast, when they take advantage of you any chance they can.

Point of all this is me encouraging you to get your own modem, get your own router and AP (or combo unit, although I prefer them separate) and pare down your ISP bill as much as you can. Stop giving them money.

Note that apparently if you get voice service through Comcast, you'll still need their combo modem unit of some sort. Well, cut that service from your monthly budget too. If we just had some competition, I'd cut Comcast out of my life completely.

Another thing is that if you have their modem and you need help with it, they may call it your responsibility and charge you for any "help" they provide. At least if you own your own stuff, you'll know if it's your problem or theirs.

Modem is straightforward and easy to use as any. If you ever download at high rates for days on end, it'll need cycled, but that's not the modem's fault; it just happens.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0

ClearStream Micron-R Indoor HDTV Antenna with Reflector - 35 Mile Range I have a roof-top antenna that worked well for analog stations but, when I converted to digital, I went from receiving 8 stations to just 1. After trying a few other antennas, I came across the ClearStream 4. I'm able to pull in 20+ digital stations perfectly, and 4 more so-so. Several analog stations come in as well, but the picture is not nearly as good as the digitial stations.

The antenna is well-made, but is a bit of a pain to assemble - lots of pieces to screw together. It only takes about 10 minutes, but you'll probably need to utter a few choice words since it's hard to get the screws to line up properly. The directions are pretty spotty, but give you the essential information. The brackets are heavy-duty, and everything is either aluminum or plastic, so it should hold up well to the elements if I put it outside. Right now, it is in my attic, and may stay there since it pulls in all the stations I want to watch. It does not come with a cable.

It's pretty compact given its performance, and much more compact that the DB8 (another Antenna Direct model with about the same specifications). Very happy with the performance. Also have a DB2 -- see my comments on that review that compare it to this antenna in terms of performance.

text_fidelity_a:
SAMSUNG 870 QVO SATA III SSD 2TB 2.5" Internal Solid State Drive, Upgrade Desktop PC or Laptop Memory and Storage for IT Pros, Creators, Everyday Users, MZ-77Q2T0B I was immediately suspicious of the box when I saw it.

It looked like the security tape had been lifted and then reapplied as can be seen in the photo I included with this review.

This was an item sold and shipped by Amazon.

I went online to watch unboxing videos of the same product so that I might be able to spot signs of a fake product when I opened it.

I called Amazon and verified that I could return the product for a refund even if opened and then took an unboxing video of it while on the phone with an Amazon rep.

I couldn't tell from looking at the drive or the rest of the packaging that anything was wrong with it.

I told the Amazon rep that I would check with Samsung the next next day to see if they could verify if it as an authentic Samsung serial number and as a new product.

I expressed my concern that even if it was a Samsung product that it might be used and I would never have any way of knowing. Or even if I could tell it was used after I installed it I would then be in the position of having to uninstall the drive in order to return it.

The Amazon rep told me that if anything was wrong with the product that Amazon would issue a refund without requiring me to return it if it was already installed in my computer.

Samsung verified the serial number the next day as being authentic and said that I could even tell if it had been used before as well by using their magician software program.

I thought the only way I would be able to detect if it was used was if there was old data on it left by someone else but Samsung said their software could detect if the drive had been written on before.

The catch is that that software can only be used to diagnose a drive after it has been installed internally to a direct SATA connection. Their software couldn't diagnose the drive through an HDMI connection to an external dock unfortunately.

Based on it having an authentic Samsung serial number, the assurance by Samsung that their software could detect both fake and used products and the assurance by the Amazon rep that I could receive a return-less refund if needed I went ahead and had the drive installed.

I figured the worst case scenario would be that it was a fake and/or non functional drive and I would have to take it out again immediately, the best case scenario was that it was a new and working Samsung drive and the in between scenario would be an authentic but used Samsung drive.

It turned out to be a used drive. It had been wiped and reformatted but it had been written to before.

I called Amazon back and told them the drive was verified as used and I expected a refund. At first the rep refused any refund and then said I would only receive a refund if I uninstalled the drive and sent it back.

I told them that was fine with me if they were willing to pay for both the installation and the uninstallation fees charged by a computer repair shop.

The Amazon rep of course refused either option so I directed him to get a suprivisor on the call and then played the recording of the conversation I had with the Amazon rep the day before....I got my refund immediately.

The big lesson here is to record the unboxing of any expensive items you buy, especially if the packaging looks tampered with or damaged.

Another lesson is to record your phone calls with Amazon reps or with any customer service person if you are calling up with an issue.

I learned a few things about this product and Amazon throughout this process.

These QVO Samsung drives store four bits of info per solid state cell. Most consumer SSD drives store only three and some expensive special purpose ones store just one.

These drives have a shorter life spans than three bits per cell drives and handle having large amounts of data written to them at slower speeds than three bits per cell drives. They should be cheaper as a result but often aren't.

Amazon has no way of tracking where a product comes from even if it was sold and shipped by them.

Amazon just puts all the Samsung 1TB 870 QVO drives into a bin regardless of whether or not Amazon bought them from Samsung directly themselves or they were supplied to Amazon by a third party seller.

Unless its an Amazon branded product that no one sells on Amazon but Amazon (Amazon basics, 365 Foods, etc) they have no way of knowing where it originally came from even if it is “sold and shipped by Amazon”.

Buyer beware.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG 870 QVO SATA III SSD 2TB 2.5" Internal Solid State Drive, Upgrade Desktop PC or Laptop Memory and Storage for IT Pros, Creators, Everyday Users, MZ-77Q2T0B

text_fidelity_a:
Sony SSCSE Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers, Black, Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers (Pair), 4 Inch (Pack of 2) I found it odd, reading some of these reviews, which claimed that these Sonys were definitely better than the Pioneer BS22s. Very odd indeed. It makes me wonder if they either weren't directly comparing the two back and forth, or didn't have the Pioneers set up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off.

To my ears, the Sonys aren't much better than the Micca MB42x. They both have slightly elevated treble, and are rather thin and one-note sounding in their presentation. Not a lot of depth or punch.

The BS22s however, you really "feel" the music. The soundstage is very open, and everything sounds larger even though the woofers are only 4" compared to the 5-1/4" SSCS5s. There is depth and a musicality that just can't be matched by the Sonys, and it's apparent right away. It's like they almost disappear and you're just left with the music. Most speakers in this price range are going to sound similar to the SSCS5/MB42x, not many if any are going to sound like the Pioneers.

I must have switched back and forth 200-300 times comparing the two, trying to convince myself that the Sonys were better than they were. I got them at $73 and the BS22s at $99, so I really wanted to like the SSCS5s.

It was always obvious which speaker was superior though - not once did I say "oh, the Sonys really sound better here". That's not to say these are bad speakers, but I don't think they're worth much more than $73, the sale price. The Pioneers however I'd be willing to pay their retail price and a bit more. If you're really on a budget, you could be satisfied with these ~$73, especially if you're only concerned about watching movies. But if you are willing to pay $20 more for the Pioneers when they're on sale (or even at $129), I'd recommend it.

Just remember to set the BS22s up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off. Also make sure they're properly amped.

The SSCS5s are decent and cheap enough that I decided to use my old receiver with them at my computer. I'd probably prefer them over the MB42X slightly, but that's about it.

With a budget sub like the Dayton SUB-1200 properly placed (subwoofer crawl) along with the BS22s, you'll have a system that sounds very nice and hits above its weight class - trust me on that. It used to be that headphones were a cheaper investment than speakers and you could get a better sound for less, but this set up edges out my HE-500/Bifrost/Asgard 2 and it's actually cheaper. Didn't think that was possible.

Sony X800H 55-inch TV: 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV with HDR and Alexa Compatibility - 2020 Model Background: I spec and integrate the highest resolution LCD’s produced in aerospace defense applications. LCD image performance is measured in hundreds of dimensions and environments. Sony is not a player in that space.

For home, I’ve been SID show and showroom shopping LCD, OLEDs, etc image quality for years. This year, I’m replacing a comparably sized exercise room 1080p LCD set. Sony has always been, to my eye, a superb comparative model and a $100 or so more than other competitors. Is the premium worth it?

This Sony X800H is an eye grabber across the showroom and on close inspection. It’s a phenomenal picture. Sony’s proprietary LCD foundries are unique in the industry. The Sony LCD foundry produces a distinctive LCD that is worth the premium price to the discerning.

Performance-wise, Sony reduced the native refresh rate to 60hz from 120hz last year. That’s quite practical as it will be some years before >60fps cameras are widely available at native 120fps. No matter, the 60hz to 120hz refresh is not discernible to the eye. The X800H imaging software can be seen to take care of latency artifacts at factory default settings … no viewing distance ghosting, inverse ghosting, blur or pulse-width modulation.

There is a comment regarding darkness, edge lighting, and illumination issues. The X800H is both edge and background light as best as I can discern without tearing it apart. It's uniform lighting no matter. Sony has always been the master of the best 'optical black' pixel to enrich the color pixel perception. The X800H is loaded with image quality controls. Image software quality defaults arrived set at factory default. It was perfect out of the box. Don't adjust anything. I rarely futz with default settings. No one should have to. The vast majority of image problems are video source input. Change the channel first and compare the image.

An old school key attribute is viewing angles … how many degrees left/right and horizontal/vertical are necessary to degrade the image. The viewing angles here are excellent. Viewing angles are a peek into the remarkable quality of Sony’s proprietary LCD foundry.

Sony’s software, firmware, Smart integration, and image processors are likewise Sony proprietary. Sony names these features like everyone else. Feature comparisons are mostly apparent in year over year Sony tech evolution.

Of course, the real story is in the final image quality. The X800H is one excellent viewing experience.

Better than advertised. Better than expected. In this size, the X800H is the benchmark, IMHO.
text_fidelity_b: Sony X800H 55-inch TV: 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV with HDR and Alexa Compatibility - 2020 Model

ASUS ZenBook 13 Ultra-Slim Laptop, 13.3” Full HD WideView, 8th Gen Intel Core i5-8265U, 8GB LPDDR3, 512GB PCIe SSD, Backlit KB, Fingerprint, Slate Gray, Windows 10, UX331FA-AS51 This review is about what I think >90% of users will care about. The detail specs are a step further, higher and faster and advertised and advertised. The Asus ZenBook 13 has been my go-to everyday toting computer for some 7-8 years.

I have last year’s i5 gen7 ZenBook 13 to directly compare the two.

P.S. This Zen-book has been so good that I had it modified to incorpoarte medical practice compliant HIPA secured software. It's a step function increase in my nightly homework replacing my 7-year old Dell. This laptop is ubiquitously practical with 180 screen twist for descirbing patient procedures. With the med-system handshacks, its like 3x faster than the Dell.

First, this new i5 gen8 ZenBook 13 has a quarter inch all-around smaller footprint. The 1/4" is immediately noticeable from last year’s edition. The 1/4" bezel is noticeably better. As small a footprint as the two have, Asus has reduced the size with no compromise in keyboard utility.

This year's ZenBook is noticeably thinner. Recharge and headphone jack are reversed. This year's hinge is slightly more robust to account for the reduced thickness. The hinge has been a 'should improve' on ZenBooks since inception. This years may solve the issue for good.

The plug-outs are changed. Make sure the output ports are what you want. For my purposes, the addition of a standard HDMI vice last year’s mini-HDMI is an improvement requiring no adapter. Last year’s SD input has been correctly reduced to the increasingly popular/common micro-SD. Plug-out needs are easily resolved with a USB-C adapter hub.

The discrete Nvidia graphics will be an interesting exploration.

The Asus fingerprint reader has never failed. This edition looks identical to last years and has been creatively moved right and off the touchpad. The ZenBook has been the very best reader compared to my HP Envy (dang good) and Dell XPS (50:50 chance).

This year's battery is new tech. The lithium-polymer battery promises up to 14 hours and includes fast-charge technology that takes "just 49 minutes" to recharge to 60% capacity. I get 11 hours out of last year’s battery every day. I can't recall running out of battery on last years on battery save mode on trans-con flights.

Wish it came with Windows Pro instead of Home, but oh well.

Finally, both last years and this year are so fast you'd have to instrument to tell a speed difference. The ZenBooks 1-2-3 second boot to Windows is 'instant' for practical purposes.

Love it. Exceeds expectations. There's no purchase mistake to be made with the UX331.

text_fidelity_a:
Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black) I bought this system to replace my Yamaha YSP-500 and a fairly sizeable subwoofer. My issue was that we were doing a remodel of our living room to put in a wall with a fireplace and stonework where our existing entertainment center was. Because the Yamaha projector is fairly substantial, mounting it directly to the wall wasn't an option, so I would have had to build another shelf or do something else. I would have also had to relocate the sub which would have meant either buying some sort of wireless set up or running a cable under the floor and into the wall.

Since the Bose speaker is much slimmer and lighter, has an available wall bracket, and the sub is wireless I thought I had the solution to my problem. For that part, the Bose is great. It was easy to mount, is relatively unobtrusive, and having more flexibility with the placement of the sub is really nice. If you have space limitations or just don't want to mess with running speaker wire (or can't) then this is a good alternative.

This is also a good alternative for people that just want to plug something in and have it work. If you are technically challenged, or just don't want to invest the time in setting up a home theater then this is a usable solution. Most people could have this up and running (including configuration) in less than 20 minutes.

I thought the sound quality is pretty decent. I don't know that it is significantly better than the older (and cheaper) Yamaha Sound Projector that it replaced. Unlike some reviewers, I thought voices (at least on television shows) were clearer and easier to hear than what I was used to. The bass was crisp, but I haven't experienced the punch I am used to with my Yamaha sub. Granted the Bose Accoustimass module is a lot smaller, but there is a very noticeable difference.

There are two areas that I took a star away for each. One is obviously cost. At around $1000, I would say that this would be a better value. At its current price I think that you are not really getting what you pay for. For all the trade-offs, I think there are cheaper alternatives.

The second is the fact that it lacks any sort of display or ability to customize. You can't make any sort of sound profiles (movies, sports, etc), you don't have anything like a night mode, and there is no display whatsoever to indicate something as simple as volume level. Some people may like that, but to me it was rather annoying. For the price, I think you should be able to do a little more with it. Again, if you are the plug-and-play type, this probably won't bother you.

Overall, other than the size and wireless sub, this is not an improvement from my Yamaha Sound Projector. I think it's good, but if I had to do it over again I would probably look at other, cheaper options.
text_fidelity_b: Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black)

I was in the market for an inexpensive dual-boot Win10/Android tablet. I researched for about a week, and I am really happy with the choice I made.

What I wanted: A 8 or 10-inch tablet that I could use for web browsing and video streaming. I game and have a nice gaming laptop that I didn't want to lug around for these purposes. I wanted a decent screen that didn't look cheap. Also the ability to play Android games.

This tablet meets all my expectations. Build is solid and feels high quality. Screen is very bright and text is clear. I had no issues getting accounts set up in Android or Win 10. Android is bare bones and has just about nothing pre-installed, which I love. I would absolutely recommend this tablet, especially at this price point.

What you don't get: No video out port. There is a pro version of this tablet if you need that option. You are not doing any major Windows gaming on this. You are not going to run any extremely resource-intensive Windows apps on this. It has a mono speaker so you aren't getting a high-end audio experience with music. If these are things you need, you will have to spend at least six times as much.
text_fidelity_b: CHUWI Hi8 8 inch Windows 10/Android 4.4 Dual Boot Tablet PC, with Features of Intel Quad Core, Full HD 19201200 IPS Screen, 2G RAM/32G ROM and Winkey

text_fidelity_a:
Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US) Though I am giving a review for this backpack, I can't come from the perspective of having used it for a while. I only received my Targus backpack yesterday, but from the looks of it I am pretty darn sure this backpack will last a long, long time. I've used MANY backpacks in the past carrying books, laptops and supplies during the time it took to earn two separate college degrees, and at my previous job of 17 years. I had to carry tools, manuals, laptops and assorted parts to calibrate monitoring equipment around my state. I was rough on the backpacks and some wore out.

I really wish I had had a backpack like this one. It's very well constructed out of strong materials, has a plethora of pockets and places to organize your stuff, and though I don't have a 17" notebook as of yet, it appears to be deep and wide and should easily fit one. There are even slots for file folders and inside zipper pouches. There are pockets on the inside and pockets on the outside. The bottom inside has a foam rubber "shock pad" that neatly folds down flat on the bottom of the backpack and is about 1/2" thick. Plus the bottom is covered in a waterproof rubbery material that should definitely help keep water from seeping up into the bag. That happened to me several times on my job with my other backpacks and it was really frustrating. It's very easy to set your backpack down on the ground not realizing the area is wet.

The shoulder straps are padded and adjustable, and it has a waist strap for extra stability. Even if you didn't use this backpack to tote your 17" marvel of technology around, it would serve well as a camper/hiker backpack. I can't wait to start using it. If something should go wrong or tear up, I will most definitely update this review telling about it, but for now I can find no fault whatsoever with it.
text_fidelity_b: Targus Demolition Backpack Designed to Fit up to 17.3-Inch Laptop, Black (TSB220US)

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy Tab (7-inch, 16GB, Wi-Fi) I really liked this 7" Tab (GT-P1010) at first. It's most useful function is web surfing.

Now, after several months of use, it's SLOOOOOOOW to load and update pages and locks up occasionally for no particular reason. I've uninstalled every unnecessary app but whether using the default Browser or Dolphin, it's more frustrating than useful.

It's also inaccurate for when inputting via keyboard. Oftentimes the keyboard adds wild characters all by itself.

Forget firmware updates. You are stuck with whatever it came with. And if you think Samsung will be any help, think again. I put "GT-P1010" in Samsung's product support page and got "no results."

I have to say Apple's major firmware updates work a whole lot better. First, because they happen at all and second, because they are seamless and reliable. Android is buggy and needs fixing on this Samsung Tablet. Samsung's "answer" is to buy a new tablet.

The device has two cameras and would be ideal for video chatting, but won't work with Skype. Apparently it needs the next version of Android. (See above concerning that impossibility.) But who knows if the next-up model will work either?

These things all want to be Apple but simply fall short.

One nice thing is that most Flash content is supported when web surfing. Apple is way lacking here. I used an iPad 1 for some time and it's pretty frustrating that it simply ignores so much content.

Bottom line is I won't buy another wannabe Samsung device like this that lacks firmware updates. (I did the same thing looking for the perfect mp3 player: everyone tried to sell the "iPod killer" and I spent more money trying to avoid the iPod. Then I bought an iPod3 and later an iPhone4 and understood how excellent their engineering and software and OS are and how with OS updates the devices continually get better even after you make the purchase.) They are too expensive to throw away and Samsung can't or won't fix the bugs. Thus you are stuck with an expensive, buggy toy that's frustrating to use. No thank you.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab (7-inch, 16GB, Wi-Fi)

Fortunately it fits just barely in my Sentey Gaming case. I had purchased the Arctic Freezer 7 Pro Rev 2 but that was far worse than the AMD 8350's included cooler fan, probably because the contact surface is designed for Intel chips and is much smaller than for AMD chips.
Be prepared for some work installing this fan as you have to install a new back-plate on the motherboard. The included parts are perfect in that they provide everything you will need including the thermal compound. So I also purchased the 2 top case fans (Corsair series). Without the cooler, the top fans did indeed reduce the top CPU temperatures by about 4C degrees - almost as though the case cover is open. With the cooler though the CPU temperature never climbed beyond 61C degrees even when all 8 cores were saturated (was compiling code). Without the cooler and the the top fans I was hitting 70C degrees which is 5 degrees above allowed operating temperature. I am surprised my AMD 8350 is still operational. With the cooler and top fans the temperature drop is 15C which is a win! Maybe I can use the Arcrtic Freezer in an Intel setup.
text_fidelity_b: Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO V2 CPU Air Cooler with SickleFlow 120, PWM Fan, Direct Contact Technology, 4 Copper Heat Pipes for AMD Ryzen/Intel LGA1700/1200/1151, Silver/Black

I like the texture on the outside of the case.
The case allows my iPad to sit on my lap and type comfortably and easily.
The case has a strong magnet that connects to the keyboard - its very easy to snap on/off.
Although I really like this case for typing, I’m not a huge fan of it for random web searching and my mindless use (Facebook, Pinterest, Instagram). I prefer a case that has a strap on the back for my hand and I like to use my iPad in vertical mode and onto horizontal. For that reason I have purchased an additional case that I use during those times.
Some features that would be nice for a future version of this product would be if when charging my iPad, it also somehow charged my keyboard. Another feature I would like would be if there was a touch pad mouse on the keyboard space. I find myself trying to use it like a laptop but that functionality isn’t there.
This laptop is high quality and feels like an actual keyboard, not a bad attempt like some iPad keyboards.
I like that I can control a lot of things directly from the keyboard like volume and Siri.
I’m very happy with this keyboard case.

It is portable enough to lug over to your buddy's house for play dates, but it is too bulky and heavy to carry to work everyday. Construction is very good with an aggressive-looking aluminum case to match the aggressive-sounding "Legion" product name. Mechanical keyboard has decent (but not the best) travel and the large keys are backlit so you can easily play your games in the dark. Dolby Atmos audio works well for games, but is kind of thin for music or movies unless you hook it up to external speakers. This Y720 version has a 1080p IPS display, which is OK but not as bright or contrasty as some other laptops I have used. There is also a more expensive 4K display available, but I have not tried that.

Core i7 CPU with 16GB of RAm gives you really great performance. This machine is easily powerful enough for any games I tried on it. Even though performance is throttled somewhat when run off the battery, battery life is still less than 2 hours under heavy use (maybe 6 hours with light use).

For the money, it is hard to go wrong with these Lenovo Legions. If you don't want to spend more than $1000, the cheaper Legion Y520 is almost as good for most types of games and costs $300 less.

text_fidelity_a:
Damero 2pcs/Set Portable Electronic Accessories Travel Organizer, Black I'll admit it right up front: I am an organizer junkie. I love having all of my things laid out perfectly and well organized in all of the different areas of my house. While I try to minimize as much as possible, if I do need to have a variety of items, and let's face it, electronics accessories and cords seem to multiply like rabbits, I want to keep them in an organized, attractive way so that I can always find what I'm looking for and so that they look nice on my shelves.

This two-piece set is meant to be a travel organizer kit for your electronics, but I'm using it in my office to keep all of the excess cords, cards, plugs, etc. for all of my various peripherals. It's fabulous, because I have one that I keep near my computer and one that I keep in my closet, depending on the frequency of use. If I need to get a cord out, it's right there, yet the cases are subtle enough that I don't feel like I'm looking at something overly functional all the time. It just looks neat, clean, and well-planned.

The quality on these is amazing. They are just stiff enough to hold their shape, yet flexible enough that if something's a little bit taller I can close the zipper over it and it's no big deal. The dividers attached by Velcro and so you can move them around so that it works perfectly around whatever it is you want to store and there. I've changed my mind a few times, and it takes two seconds to move the Velcro to hold everything perfectly in place so that it doesn't shift when you move the case around. I gave two stars because while they worked, they were amazing. I just wish they'd lasted longer.

TV Antenna - 1byone Amplified 50 Mile HDTV Digital Antenna Powerful Amplifier Signal Booster for All TV 4K UHF VHF 1080P Local Channels with 20ft Coaxial Cable This is a review of the 50 mile OUS00-0562 model. To summarize: It works. But it's no better than my cheap [[ASIN:B000HKGK8Y RCA Indoor FM and HDTV Antenna]] antenna that I was trying to replace, yet costing several times more.

With my cheap RCA "rabbit ears" antenna I was getting 18 channels, being 8 miles away from the transmitter. According to my digital-to-analog converter most TV signals were in the range of 75% to 30%. I was looking for a better antenna to improve the signal quality, so when I saw that the OUS00-0562 model was on sale I bought it. I didn't believe the 50 mile claim of this antenna since most antennas with this claim are large, more expensive and rather directional. But I figured that even if it was half that it had to be better than my RCA one. Whatever this antenna was directional of not was not specified, I assumed that it was not.

The OUS00-0562 model comes with an antenna with a 20 foot non-removable cord. This was disappointing, but I should have realized this when looking at the product pictures. Having so much cable slack is a waste when it sits 3 feet from the TV. Before I installed the 1byone antenna I took note of signal strength of each channel of my RCA antenna. The OUS00-0562 package also comes with an amplifier, which I connected to my RCA antenna as a test - and was disappointed. Only 3 channels were 10% higher, and that was within margin of error. The OUS00-0562 disappointed me soon after, as there was no change in signal strength on any channel over the RCA antenna (except that it gave me two more channels at 40% signal).

The short version:

RCA "rabbit ears" - 18 channels, 75%-30% (+/- 5%)
RCA "rabbit ears" with 1byone amplifier - 18 channels, 70%-30% (+/- 5%)
1byone OUS00-0562 with 1byone amplifier - 20 channels, 70%-30% (+/- 5%)

I tried to reposition the OUS00-0562 antenna to see if there was a directional issue, if I was out of the "sweat spot." I did notice 5-10% dips here and there but no marked improvements. I didn't spend much time on this and since it wasn't shipped with a stand. You can buy one, but I didn't want to spend any more money on it since to me it was overpriced as is. I promptly returned it.

I will give this antenna one point though. It's better looking than the RCA antenna and it takes up less space. So if looks and space matter, it might be for you.
text_fidelity_b: TV Antenna - 1byone Amplified 50 Mile HDTV Digital Antenna Powerful Amplifier Signal Booster for All TV 4K UHF VHF 1080P Local Channels with 20ft Coaxial Cable

Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black) For the non-professional photographer looking to get high-quality images in a variety of settings, this camera works great. I did a little experiment to see how it performed by taking it with me to Europe along with a much more expensive semi-professional Nikon (D3100). Here are the results:

Advantages:
-With our limited time, my camera was able to take a variety of shots (panoramic, zoom, close-up) quickly and easily while the Nikon could only take limited kinds because of the need to bring several lenses and because of the complexity (sometimes) of setting up a given shot
-Because it was small, I didn't have to lug around a big camera bag, which also had the potential of getting a little too much unwanted attention
-One feature I really enjoyed was the two simultaneous flash/no flash shot which gives you the same picture with and without flash, letting you choose later which you prefer
-Didn't need more than one lens
-With city shots of architecture, my camera fared better with its versatility

Disadvantages:
-In the mountains, the Nikon did better, capturing color and clarity/detail. In my shots, the trees looked less defined from high up. Also, his zoom lens was able to capture much more detail than my camera.
-Nature shots and portraits have slightly duller colors, missing something the other camera was able to capture
-There was slightly more blur in shots with movement with this camera

Conclusion:
For the price, this camera performed much better than I expected and was not as much of a hassle as our semi-professional camera, so for most people, this is not only going to be a better value, but less frustrating and cumbersome. For the professional, this is obviously not the best choice, but this isn't being marketed as a professional camera. This is a great family and vacation camera that everyone can use, and that still yields quality images with plenty of artistic integrity.
Great little camera, and fun to use!

**see pics for some examples of how this camera performed**
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix T300 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 10x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens (Black)

Seagate Expansion Desktop 12TB External Hard Drive HDD - USB 3.0 for PC Laptop (STEB12000400) The perfect external 3.5" hard drive for purchase at this point in time as far as I'm concerned: they include controller software *if you want it*, but they don't try to persuade you to use it, instead taking the simplistic approach, which is plug it in and use it! I would never use software to run a hard drive anyway.

Also, 4TB seems to be the sweet spot right now for price/size ratio for external 3.5" storage (3.5" drives always require an external power source, whereas 2.5" external drives - which are sometimes slower - usually do not). I like that you can leave it plugged in, but it only powers on when you attach the USB cable.

USB 3.0 really is a vast improvement over previous versions. I'm dumping all my files from five other drives on this monster, and 500GB are transferring through the computer from one drive to another in around 2-3 hours, both large and tiny files.

Worth noting is that the case seems very thin around the drive, which is probably good for heat dispersion, but will not provide the kind of protection you'd want if you were constantly transporting this drive.

I now have on here hundreds of seasons of TV shows, most in HD, nearly a thousand movies, most in HD, hundreds of music albums, books, maps, comics, software setup files, etc., and I STILL have room to grow. To get all these things consolidated and organized - and all accessible with a single drive powered up - is really fantastic.

text_fidelity_a:
Yamaha AVENTAGE RX-A880 7.2-ch 4K Ultra HD AV Receiver with HDR Dolby Vision Dolby Atmos Wi-Fi Phono YPAO and MusicCast. Works with Alexa. Update: I really love this machine. You give a lot of things five stars if they're really good products, but this one deserves bonus. I've been slowly going through the full 200+ page manual to make sure I don't miss any features and to get the most out of this thing, and I'm continually thrilled. Also, I give a lot of things controlled by apps low ratings because I tend to hate screwing around with my phone, but in this case, the Yamaha AV controller app only adds to the value, with the best part being you don't NEED it to take advantage of all the receiver's functionality, but it's a joy to have sometimes to make fine adjustments without having to turn on the TV. I really like it for adjusting net radio stations and stuff like that or fine tuning music sounds - again, without having to turn on the TV. This also makes up for the one negative I mentioned below about not being able to change all the settings from a web page. Great stuff!

Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.

And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. Sudio N2 Pro True Wireless Bluetooth in-Ear Earbuds with ANC - Multipoint Connection, IPX4 Water Resistant, USB-C and Wireless Charging, Microphone, 30h Play Time with Charging Case (Blue) I’ve used the Sudio N2 Pro Earbuds for about a month, and I like them. I typically wear them for about 2-3 hours a day while working at my desk, and I have two major pros and three major cons I’ve noticed during the last month.

PROS:
🎵 The earbuds are super comfortable! I have multiple inner ear piercings in both ears (rook, daith, tragus) and a LOT of earbuds hurt after about thirty minutes. I can wear the Sudio N2s for several hours at a time. Small, medium, and large silicone tips are included so you can get a good fit depending on your ears. Sometimes I walk around my house and do chores with these in, they haven’t fallen out once.

🎵 For earbuds, the ANC is good! I can actually notice a difference with the ANC on and off; with some earbuds that claim to have noise cancelling, there’s really no difference. The ANC on the Sudio N2s blocks out when the television is playing in the next room, and even muffles the sound of the heater right under my desk.

CONS:
🎵 Battery life is not great. With ANC on, I get 4 hours, maaaaybe 4.5 if I’m lucky. I put the case on my charging pad every other day, it seems. The case supports wireless charging, which is a positive, or via USB-C. I’ve noticed the earbuds don’t always turn off when put in the case and the lid is closed, which undoubtedly contributes to the faster battery drain.

🎵 The earbuds support Multipoint connection, or connecting to multiple devices, but I can only get them to connect to my Mac. No matter what I try, they will not connect to my phone (Samsung Note 20 Ultra). I tried every suggestion in the online manual, but I can’t even get the earbuds to factory reset.

🎵 The touch controls are VERY sensitive. I have to make sure I don’t have any video tabs open when I put them in, or the video starts blasting in my ear. The only audible cue I noticed was to turn ANC on, and that is “Noise Cancelling.” A beep indicates turning it off, and beeps are used for all other cues. I don’t know what does what, I just wish I could turn them off.

Although the cons slightly outweigh the pros, I still use the Sudio N2s every day. The comfort is a huge factor for me. I’ve tried probably 8 pairs of earbuds in the last year, and this is the only pair I can wear for more than an hour at a time.
text_fidelity_b: Sudio N2 Pro True Wireless Bluetooth in-Ear Earbuds with ANC - Multipoint Connection, IPX4 Water Resistant, USB-C and Wireless Charging, Microphone, 30h Play Time with Charging Case (Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology This is a cameras that is perfect for some but not something that everyone will find useful. The ideal user is someone who wants a simple to use digital camera that has the ability to instantly print the photo without dealing with a PC or conventional printer. This does a pretty good job of accomplishing that goal. But, if you’re looking for a more advanced point and shoot with lots of image features, this may not be your best option.

The camera itself feels very solid, but lacks a key digital camera feature: a view screen. At first glance may seem to be a major omission. But, this camera is designed to be a high-tech replacement for the old-style Polaroid instant cameras by instantly (well, relatively instantly) printing the photo on Zink paper. Note that the paper needs to be purchased separately, and is pretty much an essential component for using the camera. While you can store photos on an SD card, the camera is really designed to be used with the Zink paper.

Usage is very straightforward – it’s about as point and shoot as you can get. That’s great for those who don’t want to fiddle with any settings, but it does put some constraints on image quality. I’ve had about 20% of my photos so far turn out less than ideal due to improper focus, poor white balance, poor resolution and/or incorrect color registration. That’s my major complaint with this camera – the paper is costly, and when you have to toss (or at least not really like) one in five photos, the cost can add up.

The images are small – the paper is only 2 by 3 inches. On the plus side it has a peel and stick backing, so you can use the photos as “post-its” very easily. Again, this is keeping with the intent of the camera, so I won’t downgrade the rating due to the small photo size.

Other negatives for me is that the battery is not user-replaceable. I’ve had too many electronic products with built-in batteries that had to be trashed since the internal battery no longer held a charge. I’m also not fond of the lens cap. It’s very easy to take off (it’s held in place by magnets) but there’s no attachment to the camera, so it’s very easy to misplace.

But this does score well with regard to ease of use and fun. As a test of ease of use I handed this to my Mom who is technically challenged, to say the least. She had no problems snapping photos and loved having the image print right there. She’s never liked using a digital camera in the past due to difficulty using it and dealing with image files. This was right up her ally.

While I’ll drop the rating to 4 stars due to the image quality issues that can crop up, overall this is a unique camera. It’s not right for everyone, but if you’re looking to revisit the days of the Polaroid instant camera while staying in the digital world, this is well worth considering.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Zink Polaroid Snap Instant Digital Camera (Pink) with ZINK Zero Ink Printing Technology

1MORE iBFree In-Ear Earphones Wireless Headphones with Bluetooth 4.2 AAC, IPX 6 Waterproof, Secure Fit, In-Line Mic for Sports Gym Running - New Model Black I don't know what to think of these headphones. The sound out of the box is terrible, just abysmal. I've never heard a more unbalanced headphone anywhere. If you can't use an eq with these headphones, stop reading and look elsewhere.

If you can use an eq in your application, you might find these headphones surprising. Once the shrill high-end is toned down and the bass and mids bumped up, you will find the sound is pretty good for a ~$60/pair. The soundstage is small, but clear and the instrument separation surpasses what I was expecting. However, boost the bass too much and you will get distortion.

A couple of weeks before buying these I heard the quad-driver version and they were simply amazing. It was like I was sitting in my own living room listening to a full surround sound setup. I've never heard spacial definition or as big a soundstage in a headphone as I did with the quad-drivers, especially IEMs. The quad-drivers are on par with $600/pair HiFiMan planars. That's why I took a chance on this much cheaper bluetooth version of a single driver.

If you don't mind playing with the eq and don't want to buy cheap knock-offs from china (these are made in china, but by the company that designed them), take a chance on these. If you just want to plug and play, buy something else. I'm still on the fence on returning them myself.
text_fidelity_b: 1MORE iBFree In-Ear Earphones Wireless Headphones with Bluetooth 4.2 AAC, IPX 6 Waterproof, Secure Fit, In-Line Mic for Sports Gym Running - New Model Black
